sections.html:
• Other names: leaf slug, leaf sheep, sap-sucking sea slug, salty ocean caterpillar
  • Optimal tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Specific gravity: 1.021–1.025
  • KH: 7–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: photosynthetic / algae eater
  • Temperament: reef safe / peaceful
  • Colour: green

Costasiella kuroshimae is scarce in the aquarium trade, probably because most aquarists are unfamiliar with the species or cannot cope with its demands. It is rarely found at local fish stores, and the price is unknown.

It should only be acquired by those willing to give it special care, since it cannot thrive on other food items and cannot survive in a tank full of aggressive tankmates. Its downsides are its preference for a specific type of green macroalgae, its susceptibility to predators and its short lifespan in captivity.

Costasiella kuroshimae was discovered in 1993 off the coast of Kuroshima, Japan; its name refers to the type locality Kuroshima in Okinawa, Ryukyu Islands. It is found on reefs off the coasts of Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines.

Taxonomy: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Mollusca, Class Gastropoda, Clade Heterobranchia, Clade Sacoglossa, Family Costasiellidae, Genus Costasiella.
This sea slug inhabits shallow saltwater environments with ample green macroalgae.

Because of their small size, there is no minimum requirement. However, in a small tank it is difficult to keep constant control over water parameters, and everything can go wrong very fast. A tank of at least 40 litres is suggested. At the same time, these slugs are so small that they will be lost in a big tank.

• Temperature: 22–27°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Specific gravity: 1.023–1.025
  • Calcium: 380–450 ppm
  • Magnesium: 1200–1350 ppm

Standard reef aquarium water parameters should be maintained, with ample lighting for the slug's photosynthetic activity.
Due to the tiny size of this slug, it may get sucked into overflows if there is a strong current in the tank, so keep water movement low.

Costasiella kuroshimae is an obligate algae eater. It nibbles on the green alga Avrainvillea, sucking out and retaining the functional chloroplasts in its body so it can photosynthesise later. This lets it obtain energy by photosynthesis when its main food is scarce, though the exact duration is unknown. According to one study, it can survive about 10 days without food in a natural day/night cycle.

Green macroalgae must be available in the reef tank, and not just any kind: in the wild it is commonly found grazing and resting on the seaweed Avrainvillea. Some biologists believe it is limited to a single food source.

The slug is about 3 mm to 1 cm long. It has small black beady eyes and two sensitive rhinophores (white with black tips, bearing fine hairs that sense chemicals in the water and help locate food) on its white head, resembling a sheep's ears. Its back carries rows of leaf-shaped cerata, generally green with iridescent dots and white/pink tips.

It can photosynthesise through kleptoplasty, stealing chloroplasts from the algae it eats. Its large surface area and translucent skin help maximise light capture.

It is often wrongly called a nudibranch. It belongs to Sacoglossa (sap-sucking sea slugs), not Nudibranchia, and Sacoglossans have a single row of sharp teeth on the radula adapted for sucking.

It is reef safe: there are no reports of it harming corals. It is very small and defenceless against predators, so lobsters, crabs, sea cucumbers, wrasses and some shrimp (such as coral banded shrimp and pistol shrimp) must not be kept with it. Keep it with peaceful fish that show little interest in slugs. It camouflages on seaweed and secretes mucus as a deterrent.

There are no reports of breeding in captivity. The species is hermaphroditic: two individuals mate in the water, one (acting as the male) inserting its genital organ into the female genital pore of the other. Fertilisation is internal and eggs are laid in ribbons. They hatch after a few days, releasing free-swimming veliger larvae that undergo metamorphosis into sea slugs.
Costasiella kuroshimae is difficult to keep because it is particular about its food and very picky about tankmates, which is the main reason it is not popular in reefkeeping.
